Part 1

✂️Divide, conquer, combine

A huge pile of exam papers is easier to sort with friends. Split the pile in two, give each half to a friend, and when both hand back a sorted half, merge them. Each friend can split their half again. That is divide and conquer: split a problem into smaller copies of itself, solve the copies, and combine their answers.

✂️ Divide

Cut the input into parts, usually two halves.

⚔️ Conquer

Solve each part recursively. Tiny parts are base cases.

🧩 Combine

Build the answer for the whole from the answers of the parts.

Backtracking explores choices and undoes them. Divide and conquer splits the input, and the parts never overlap. When parts do overlap, use dynamic programming instead.
Part 2

🔀Merge sort that counts: inversions

An inversion is a pair that is out of order: a bigger number before a smaller one. Counting all pairs takes O(n²). Merge sort counts them for free. When a value from the right half is merged before values still waiting in the left half, it jumps over all of them, and each jump is one inversion.

Music apps use inversions to compare two people's rankings of the same songs. Few inversions means similar taste. The Arrays chapter animates plain merge sort and quick sort step by step.
Part 3

📐How fast is it? The master theorem

A divide and conquer running time looks like T(n) = a · T(n / b) + f(n): a sub problems, each b times smaller, plus f(n) work to divide and combine. Draw the recursion tree. Level i has ai nodes, each of size n / bi. Who does most of the work, the root or the leaves, decides the answer.

AlgorithmRecurrenceWho winsResult
Binary searchT(n / 2) + 1every level equalO(log n)
Merge sort2 T(n / 2) + nevery level equalO(n log n)
Karatsuba3 T(n / 2) + nthe leavesO(n1.585)
Finding the max2 T(n / 2) + 1the leavesO(n)
Quickselect, averageT(n / 2) + nthe rootO(n)
Compare a with bd, where f(n) = nd. Equal means every level does the same work, O(nd log n). Bigger means the leaves win, O(nlogb a). Smaller means the root wins, O(nd).
Part 4

🎯Quickselect: find the k-th without sorting

To find the median of a list you do not need it fully sorted. Partition around a pivot as in quick sort, so the pivot lands at its final index. If that is the index you want, stop. Otherwise the answer is on one side only, so throw the other side away and repeat. Quick sort recurses into both sides. Quickselect recurses into one.

⚡ Average O(n)

With a fair pivot the part that is kept halves each round: n + n/2 + n/4 + ... is less than 2n comparisons.

🎲 Pick a random pivot

An unlucky pivot every time, like the last element of a sorted list, gives O(n²). A random pivot makes that very unlikely.

Part 5

📈Maximum subarray: the run that crosses the middle

Which run of neighbouring numbers has the largest sum? Split the list in half. The best run is either entirely in the left half, entirely in the right half, or it crosses the middle. The first two are smaller copies of the problem. The crossing run is easy: grow it left from the middle and right from the middle, keeping the best totals.

This runs in O(n log n). Kadane's scan solves it in O(n) and appears in the LeetCode practice to check the answer. The divide and conquer version still matters, because the same idea powers segment trees, which answer the best run in any range quickly.
Part 6

📍The closest pair of points

Given points on a map, which two are closest? Checking every pair costs O(n²). Divide and conquer sorts the points by x and splits them with a vertical line. Solve each side, and let d be the smaller answer. A closer pair across the line must have both points within d of the line, in a narrow strip. Sorted by y, each strip point only needs a few neighbours checked.

🔢 Squared distances

Comparing squared distances avoids square roots, so every number stays a whole number and all languages print the same result.

⏱️ O(n log n)

A geometry argument shows each strip point has at most 7 useful neighbours, so the strip costs O(n) per level.

Part 7

✖️Karatsuba: multiply with three products, not four

School multiplication of two n digit numbers takes n² digit products. Split each number in half: x = a · 10m + b and y = c · 10m + d. Then x · y needs ac, bd and ad + bc. The trick is that (a + b)(c + d) − ac − bd = ad + bc, so three products are enough instead of four.

Saving one product out of four sounds small, but it happens at every level: 3log₂ n = n1.585 instead of n². Python uses Karatsuba for very large whole numbers.
